title: The Devil Wears Prada 2
synopsis: Print is dead. Miranda Priestly is not. She has summoned you back to Runway — fifteen years older, a real career later, and with a daughter you can't be late to pick up. The September issue is a relaunch. Try not to fall apart.

nodes.text: An assistant's email — 'Miranda would like to see you Tuesday.' Two sentences. No subject. You read it three times in your kitchen with a child's lunchbox in your other hand.

choices.text: Reply immediately to confirm
choices.consequence: Don't hesitate; she'll notice.

choices.text: Wait a day; you have a life now
choices.consequence: Set the tone.

nodes.text: The lobby smells the same. Your heart, embarrassingly, knows the elevator buttons. Miranda's office is unchanged except for an iPad where the magazines used to be.

choices.text: Compliment the iPad
choices.consequence: Disarm with charm.

choices.text: Wait until she speaks
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Old skill—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: School drop-off Wednesday. Your daughter Beatrix asks, casually, if you're going back to that 'shouty job.' You realize she has been listening more carefully than you thought.

choices.text: Tell her about the meeting
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Honest.

choices.text: Tell her it's just lunch
choices.consequence: “Tell her it's just lunch” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Soften.

nodes.text: Miranda offers you Editor at Large for the relaunch — print plus, a quarterly object that is also a digital ecosystem. The salary is, embarrassingly, real. She does not, of course, mention the work-life balance.

choices.text: Negotiate for hours that fit your life
choices.consequence: Set the terms.

choices.text: Take the job and figure it out
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Old instinct.

nodes.text: An old colleague at a serious magazine offers you a steadier, less prestigious gig at half the salary. The two offers arrive in the same week, which is funny because life is funny.

choices.text: Take the steadier job
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Family-shaped career.

choices.text: Take Miranda's job; you can survive her now
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Risk—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: Emily Charlton — now a major brand executive — walks into Miranda's office to consult on the relaunch. She sees you. She, unusually, smiles for a second before correcting.

choices.text: Approach Emily like an old friend
choices.consequence: “Approach Emily like an old friend” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Try.

choices.text: Approach Emily as a future colleague
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Professional.

nodes.text: Beatrix, ten, asks, 'Did you have a fun day at work?' You realize she has been told that adults should have fun at work. You think about how to answer. You think for too long.

choices.text: Tell her some days are fun and some aren't
choices.consequence: “Tell her some days are fun and some aren't” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Honest.

choices.text: Tell her you'll have more fun days now
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Tell her you'll have more fun days now” back. Reassure shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: The plan is ambitious, expensive, and unlikely. Miranda wants a quarterly print object that costs a hundred dollars and sells out. She wants you to make the lead feature feel like a manifesto and a fashion shoot at once.

choices.text: Pitch a story about the daughters of fashion editors
choices.consequence: Make it personal.

choices.text: Pitch a story about climate-positive supply chains
choices.consequence: Make it political.

nodes.text: Your husband — who has, mercifully, stayed kind — looks at the calendar with you. The math is tight. The math is, with adjustments, possible.

choices.text: Adjust the math together
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Co-build.

choices.text: Take a month to test the new schedule before committing
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Trial—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: You hire a photographer Miranda hates. The photographer is brilliant. The shoot goes long. Miranda comes onto set in the last hour and is, for thirty seconds, silent. Then she says, 'Continue.' That is, in her language, applause.

choices.text: Send the photographer a handwritten note
choices.consequence: “Send the photographer a handwritten note” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Mentor up.

choices.text: Move on to the next shoot with confidence
choices.consequence: You commit to “Move on to the next shoot with confidence.” The story records the instinct as “Compound” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: The supply-chain feature is going to be the first piece many of your old fashion friends actually read. It will also, you realize, anger several advertisers. You decide that's okay.

choices.text: Run it on the cover
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Bold—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Run it as the lead of the inside well
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Strategic—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: On a school holiday Beatrix comes to the office. Miranda meets her. They shake hands gravely. Miranda compliments Beatrix's shoes. Beatrix asks Miranda, with terrifying calm, what the office is for.

choices.text: Let Miranda answer
choices.consequence: Let it land.

choices.text: Answer for both of you
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Bridge.

nodes.text: Nigel — now in a corner office somewhere else — has started a chat with Emily and you. It is, weirdly, the place you tell your worst day to people who already understand. You realize this support network is part of what makes the work survivable now.

choices.text: Use the chat as a daily lifeline
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Lean.

choices.text: Use it sparingly; don't drain it
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Steward it—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: The relaunch sells out in eleven days. Three of the climate features get picked up by serious newspapers. Miranda smiles, once, on the way to the elevator. It is, for you, the proof.

choices.text: Stay on for the next issue
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Continue—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Make a longer-term commitment
choices.consequence: You commit to “Make a longer-term commitment.” The story records the instinct as “Lock in” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: You leave the launch party at 11. Your husband and Beatrix are still up — they ordered pizza. You sit on the floor with them and eat cold slices in your dress. It is the best thirty minutes of the month.

choices.text: Make this the routine — leave early on purpose
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Build—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Take Beatrix to the next launch
choices.consequence: Bring her in.

nodes.text: Year two of the new Runway is harder. The novelty fades. The advertisers ebb and return. You and Emily and Nigel form, accidentally, a kind of cabinet around Miranda. She does not, of course, acknowledge it. She also doesn't fire any of you.

choices.text: Take the editor-in-chief role when offered
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Step up.

choices.text: Stay as Editor at Large and write more
choices.consequence: Stay in the work you love.

nodes.text: Beatrix, at twelve, decides she wants to write — not for fashion, for science. You help her get an internship at a nature magazine. You realize, gratefully, that the magazine industry has, for the next generation, gotten a little more interesting because of people like Beatrix.

choices.text: Mentor a new generation through her
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Mentor a new generation through her” back. Pay forward shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Stay focused on your own work
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Stay focused on your own work” back. Your lane shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: Miranda announces her retirement at a private lunch. She looks at you when she says it. Emily looks at you when she says it. Nigel looks, sweetly, at his salad.

choices.text: Volunteer for the role
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Volunteer for the role” back. Take it shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Volunteer Emily
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Generous—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: You drop Beatrix at the nature magazine. She is, somehow, less nervous than you. The editor shakes her hand and yours and says, 'We've heard.' You realize, on the walk back, that you have raised a person.

choices.text: Take the afternoon off to mark it
choices.consequence: You commit to “Take the afternoon off to mark it.” The story records the instinct as “Honor” and carries it forward.

choices.text: Go back to work changed
choices.consequence: “Go back to work changed” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Carry it.

nodes.text: The next September cover is being built. The decisions about it sit on your desk. You realize the cover is, in effect, a vote about who you want to be for the next decade.

choices.text: Take the EIC role and build the next decade
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Take the EIC role and build the next decade” back. Lead shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Stay Editor at Large and write the better book
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Write.

nodes.text: You become the next editor-in-chief. Miranda, in retirement, sends you a single handwritten note: 'Don't be me. Be better.' You frame it. You try.

You stay in the role that lets you write and live. You publish, in your fifties, a collection of essays about fashion and labor that gets a quiet, deserved prize. Beatrix sits in the front row at the ceremony.
